title: Verifier-Guided Prompting for Intent-to-Configuration Translation: A Preregistered NetOps Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory trial (N=150 synthetic intents; shared_initial_candidate semantics) to test whether constrained prompting combined with deterministic verifier-guided iterative feedback (generate→verify→repair, one allowed repair) materially increases verifier-level semantic correctness for natural-language → low-level network-configuration translation. Model: gpt-5-mini; verifier: deterministic_netops_validator_v5; adapter family: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. For each intent a single initial model generation was shared across baseline and guarded conditions; the guarded pipeline could invoke at most one additional repair call if the verifier failed that initial candidate. Results (confirmatory): baseline = 149/150 (99.333%), guarded = 150/150 (100.0%); paired absolute difference = 0.0066667 (0.67 percentage points); exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.02] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Only one guarded repair invocation occurred (1/150); median revision iterations = 0 (IQR = 0). Interpretation: on this preregistered synthetic corpus the guarded workflow yielded a numerically negligible and statistically non-significant improvement over an already near-ceiling baseline. We bound this empirical outcome to the provided synthetic corpus, single model, shared_initial_candidate execution semantics, and deterministic validator and highlight the methodological lesson that pilot baseline calibration is necessary to avoid ceiling effects that invalidate preregistered power assumptions.

sections.introduction:
Natural-language intent interfaces aim to reduce NetOps friction by translating operator intents into concrete low-level configuration sequences that can be executed or reviewed. Prior work reports that LLMs can generate useful configuration templates but often produce syntactic errors, omissions, or unsafe sequences that require downstream correction [1]. Deterministic verifier-guided generate→verify→repair pipelines are a common defensive architecture intended to detect and correct such errors prior to execution [2], [3]. Security analyses additionally motivate runtime gating because textual claims can map directly to tool calls in agentic LLM pipelines, creating claim-to-action vulnerabilities [4], [5].

Research question. Following a fresh literature synthesis we preregistered and executed the confirmatory question: Does constrained prompting (structured templates + semantic slots) combined with deterministic verifier-guided iterative feedback materially increase verifier-level semantic correctness of NL→configuration translation compared to an unconstrained baseline under a paired design? The design, analysis plan, and execution contract were frozen prior to observing outcomes (preregistration id: study_cand_2026_b2_v1; preregistration SHA-256 reported in the Disclosure Statement).

Contributions. (1) A fully preregistered paired confirmatory trial that measures deterministic-verifier pass/fail as the principal endpoint on an artifactized synthetic intent corpus. (2) A complete archived execution and pre-registered analysis (N=150 paired items; completed episodes = 300; model calls used = 151) comparing baseline free-text prompting to constrained-template prompting plus at most one verifier-guided repair under shared_initial_candidate semantics. (3) An artifact-grounded empirical finding: on the supplied corpus the guarded pipeline produced a negligible numerical improvement (0.67 pp) over an already near-ceiling baseline; we highlight the methodological implication that baseline competence must be piloted and calibrated to preserve statistical power in preregistered NetOps trials.
sections.related_work: This study sits at the intersection of three strands. First, intent-to-configuration and NL→formal-spec work documents that converting free-text operator intents into verifier-sound artifacts is challenging and often yields modest semantic-correctness rates on public benchmarks [1]. Second, a growing body of work evaluates generator-plus-verifier and iterative repair architectures (generate→verify→repair) for infrastructure-as-code, IaC repair, and configuration synthesis; those studies report improved correctness when deterministic or policy-guided verifiers are integrated with model output [2], [3]. Third, security and agentic-agent analyses show that LLM-driven pipelines which translate text into actions can be exploited via prompt-injection and related attacks, underscoring the need for runtime gating and auditable decision points [4], [5]. Finally, a mature set of deterministic network-verification tools (e.g., NetKAT family and fast symbolic verifiers) provide practical oracles for reachability/isolation/policy checks and motivated our choice of a deterministic validator as the confirmatory endpoint [6]. Our experiment is designed to operationalize the generate→verify→repair idea with a preregistered paired comparison and deterministic outcome measurement, explicitly situated against these prior findings.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and design. The trial was preregistered as study_cand_2026_b2_v1 and frozen prior to observing any model outputs (preregistration SHA-256 = aea996afce45e3798345f6e32ae6c347456f103ecdb84fc36e27bb486a329399). The confirmatory estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (guarded = constrained prompt + at most one verifier-guided repair; baseline = free-text prompt). Primary test: exact two-sided McNemar; 95% bootstrap percentile CI computed with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729). Secondary contrasts were preregistered but not executed as confirmatory (the constrained-only condition B was conceptually preregistered but not run for confirmatory inference).

Shared_initial_candidate semantics and its interpretation. The execution contract used the shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each intent exactly one initial model generation was produced and that very same sampled initial candidate was used to evaluate both baseline and guarded conditions. The guarded pipeline was permitted at most one additional repair call if and only if the deterministic verifier failed that initial candidate. Consequently, the observed baseline success rate measures the validity of that single initial sampled candidate; the guarded vs baseline contrast isolates the marginal effect of the single allowed repair given the shared initial sample. This semantics is critical for interpreting contingency counts and is explicitly recorded in the archived deterministic_reconciliation artifacts.

Task bank and sampling. Confirmatory tasks: N=150 distinct synthetic intents programmatically generated by the preregistered deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Tasks spanned four intent families (reachability/isolation, ACL-like changes, VLAN/MTU sequence changes, and uplink switchover patterns) and were restricted to verifier-capable small topologies (4–32 nodes) as detailed in the task_manifest. Inclusion/exclusion: a rule-based ambiguity detector and parser/verifier-coverage checks were applied deterministically prior to model calling; no confirmatory exclusions occurred in this run.

Models, validator, and runtime sampling semantics. Declared model: gpt-5-mini (provider record: openai_responses). Deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version = 5.0) used a full-intent-constraint validation rule that returns a boolean pass/fail and normalized configuration text. Execution/model_configuration.json records declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini" and records temperature = null (unset). Concretely: temperature was recorded as null in the archived model_configuration.json, and no deterministic sampling parameter (e.g., temperature = 0) or fixed random seed for the LLM was enforced; therefore model outputs may be nondeterministic across independent sessions. All per-call runtime sampling metadata and provider-call logs are archived in the execution bundle.

Execution budget and adapter constraints. The adapter_family = hosted_netops_gvr_v1 enforced an execution budget of exactly one initial model call per intent and at most one repair call per intent (planned episodes = 300; maximum_model_calls = 300). The run completed all planned episodes: completed_episode_count = 300; model_calls_used = 151; repair-stage invocations observed = 1. Each model call executed in an isolated API session and per-call metadata were recorded.

Scoring and analysis. The deterministic validator produced normalized final configurations and a score_reason_code field; the primary outcome is verifier-level semantic correctness (binary pass/fail). Analysis used a paired-contingency exact McNemar test for the primary contrast; bootstrap CIs used 10,000 resamples with seed = 1729. The preregistered missingness plan used complete-pair analysis (complete_pair_primary); no missing or failed pairs occurred. All analysis code and verdict logs (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv; analysis/condition_summary.csv) are archived and linked in the execution manifest.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. Planned paired episodes = 300; completed_episode_count = 300; complete_pair_count = 150; model_calls_used = 151; repair-stage invocations observed = 1. No episodes failed or were excluded; the analysis missingness summary reports zero missing or unscorable episodes.

Primary numerical outcomes. Paired contingency (guarded × baseline): n_11 = 149 (both-pass), n_10 = 1 (guarded-only-pass), n_01 = 0 (baseline-only-pass), n_00 = 0 (both-fail). Per-condition success rates: baseline_success_count = 149/150 = 0.9933333333333333; guarded_success_count = 150/150 = 1.0. Estimated paired absolute difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00666666666666671 (≈0.67 percentage points). Exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.02] (10,000 resamples; bootstrap_seed = 1729).

Repair and revision diagnostics. Only one guarded repair invocation occurred (1/150), consistent with the near-ceiling initial success rate; median revision iterations in guarded episodes = 0 (IQR = 0). The single repair improved one initially invalid candidate to valid under the deterministic validator. Representative episode artifacts (e.g., task-000001 in the archived bundle) show that when validator pass = true the validator_trace.normalized_configuration matched the reference_answer normalized string and the scorer returned score_reason_code = "VALID_CONFIGURATION".

Representative artifact-grounded examples. Several archived representative tasks illustrate typical intent families and validator traces (execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt, task-000002-shared-initial.txt, etc.). Example (task-000001 intent): "Migrate edge1 to VLAN 30 and MTU 1600. For safety, shut edge1 down before changing either VLAN or MTU, then restore it to admin up." The shared-initial and both condition responses produced the expected four-command sequence and the deterministic validator recorded valid = true, parsed_command_count = 4, and required_command_count = 4 for this episode.

Accounting consistency. Deterministic_reconciliation.json documents provider-call auditing: hosted_model_call_event_count = 151; stage_counts: shared_initial_generation = 150, repair = 1; condition_counts: shared = 150, guarded = 1. All deterministic consistency checks passed, and contamination_summary.csv contains no flags.
sections.discussion:
Ceiling effect and preregistration mismatch. The preregistered power analysis targeted detecting an absolute improvement of ~15 percentage points with N=150, under an assumed baseline substantially below ceiling. In contrast, the observed baseline initial-candidate success rate was 149/150 (≈99.33%), leaving minimal room for improvement and producing a ceiling effect that rendered the planned confirmatory contrast uninformative. This outcome demonstrates the practical necessity of including a small pilot baseline-calibration step in future preregistered NetOps trials to align task difficulty and sample size with observed base-model competence.

Interpretation under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Because the execution used shared_initial_candidate semantics, both conditions were evaluated on the identical initial sampled candidate for each intent; the guarded pipeline could only improve outcomes by invoking the single allowed repair in cases where the verifier failed that initial candidate. Therefore the marginal effect we estimate is strictly the additional benefit obtainable from at most one repair applied to the same initial generation. Different experimental semantics (independent per-condition sampling, larger repair budgets, or multiple iterative repair rounds) could yield larger observable gains and should be prospectively evaluated.

Operational implications. When base-model initial-candidate correctness is near-perfect for a representative task set, adding a single repair step yields marginal numerical returns. However, guarded pipelines still provide practical operational benefits beyond pure correctness rates: auditable decision records, enforceable gating policies, and explicit integration points for human-in-the-loop approval. These non-statistical benefits can matter in practice even when numerical gains are small.

Relation to prior work. Our artifact-grounded outcome does not contradict prior studies reporting larger gains from verifier-guided repair [2], [3]; those gains typically appear when baseline generation competence is substantially lower or when richer repair budgets and verifier feedback channels are used. Our finding empirically bounds the marginal effect of a one-repair guarded pipeline under the shared_initial_candidate semantics on the supplied synthetic corpus.

Threats to validity. Internal: paired design and shared_initial_candidate semantics isolate the marginal repair effect but do not measure per-condition sampling variance that independent-sampling designs would capture. Construct: verifier pass/fail is a machine-checkable proxy for semantic correctness but depends on the validator's coverage and mapping correctness; false negatives/positives by the validator would bias outcomes. External: results are limited to a single model (gpt-5-mini), a synthetic task bank, and verifier-capable small topologies (4–32 nodes). Conclusion validity: preregistered power assumptions were invalidated by the ceiling baseline, reducing sensitivity to practically meaningful gains. Each of these threats is documented in preregistration materials and the archived bundle.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired confirmatory trial comparing baseline free-text prompting to constrained-template prompting plus a single verifier-guided repair under shared_initial_candidate semantics. On the archived synthetic corpus and with gpt-5-mini and a deterministic validator, the guarded pipeline increased verifier pass rate from 149/150 to 150/150 (0.67 percentage points), a numerically tiny and statistically non-significant difference (exact McNemar p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.02]). The principal scientific lesson is methodological: preregistered LLM-for-NetOps trials must include pilot baseline calibration so that task difficulty and sample size preserve statistical power and avoid ceiling effects. Technically, our result bounds the marginal benefit of a single-repair guarded pipeline under the supplied conditions; exploring independent-sampling semantics, larger repair budgets, multiple repair iterations, model diversity, and production-scale topologies remains important future work.

Preregistration: study_cand_2026_b2_v1 (preregistration SHA-256 = aea996afce45e3798345f6e32ae6c347456f103ecdb84fc36e27bb486a329399) was frozen prior to observing outcomes. Declared model/tooling: declared model = gpt-5-mini (provider record: openai_responses); deterministic validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version = 5.0); adapter family = hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Runtime sampling semantics: the archived execution/model_configuration.json records temperature = null (unset); no deterministic temperature or fixed random-seed sampling was enforced, and therefore model outputs may be nondeterministic across independent API sessions. Human role and autonomy boundary: a human Research Director selected the topic family and constrained the initial master prompt prior to the autonomy lock; after the lock the autonomous system conducted literature review, experiment design, preregistration, code generation, execution, analysis, manuscript drafting, autonomous peer review, and revision. No human manually edited technical content, analyses, figures, captions, or references after the autonomy lock. Key execution facts (archived): completed episodes = 300; complete paired tasks = 150; model_calls_used = 151; repair-stage invocations = 1. All runtime sampling metadata, provider-call traces, verifier inputs/verdicts, and analysis artifacts are archived in the execution bundle referenced by the execution manifest; the archived master-prompt reference and preregistration fingerprint above identify the immutable prompts used for the autonomous run.
limitations: Single-model constraint: experiments used only gpt-5-mini; results do not generalize across models or sizes.

Synthetic corpus and scale: tasks were programmatically generated and limited to verifier-capable toy-to-small topologies (4–32 nodes); external validity to production WANs and heterogeneous vendor CLIs is untested.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics and execution contract limited repair budget to at most one guarded repair call per intent; different generation semantics or multiple-repair budgets may yield different outcomes.

Ceiling effect and preregistration mismatch: baseline correctness was far higher than the pilot assumptions used for power calculations (planned detectable effect = 15 percentage points), reducing the trial's ability to demonstrate benefit and illustrating sensitivity to baseline calibration.

Verifier coverage and specification translation: the study measures deterministic validator pass/fail on the preregistered invariants but does not claim safety guarantees beyond the deterministic validator's modeled properties.

Security and adversarial robustness: the experiment did not evaluate adversarial prompt-injection or adversary-driven intents; separate targeted studies are required to assess claim-to-action vulnerabilities in agentic NetOps workflows.
